conclusion: Null result for the experiment variable (none changed; reanalysis only, 0 AWS calls). Lambda CPU placement is NOT controlled. 21,160 recorded invocations in 10 runs drew CPU parts 0xd0c, 0xd40, 0xd4f; 10 runs drew all of them. Share by run: cold 0xd0c 4.0%-18.5%, cold 0xd4f 5.0%-14.5%, warm 0xd0c 1.0%-12.0%. Restores ran on 0xd0c, 0xd40 only; all 174 published versions built snapshots on 0xd0c+0xd40. A part is fixed per environment: 0 of 3,138 environments and 0 of 3,939 log streams showed two. Same-code control pool (E1, E5, P1), warm probe request engine p50: 0xd0c/0xd40 = 1.781x. Within-run arm comparisons: 16 mix_shift and 1 sign_flip of 188, where the pooled delta differs from every within-part delta by more than 1% of the control median. Valid comparisons: within one CPU part, arms in the same rounds, part mix reported. No processor generation is inferred from a part ID. Unknown for every source run: feature flags, HWCAPs, MIDR, cgroup limits, core count, kernel, AZ, physical host; the baseline harness now records them per environment (hostinfo.py, not yet run on Lambda). Fixed-host reference: P3's existing offline arm64 DevSpace (part 0xd40), labelled fixed-host, not Lambda latency. Concat 5.3%/5.6% (Lambda, sampler) vs 2.65% (offline, same sampler) vs 1.16% (offline, perf): same code and part ID, so not attributable to code; host conditions unrecorded, open. Restore latency from pooled-client runs is suspect.

concat_gap.question: P3 found ggml_compute_forward_concat at 5.3% (run 20261020T124451Z, lkaisamp, warm, part 0xd40) / 5.6% (rerun 20261020T231634Z) of Lambda CPU samples against 1.2% offline under perf and 2.65% offline under the same sampler. Host or code?

offline.host: arm64 DevSpace, part 0xd40, kernel 6.1.188, 16 CPUs, 6 threads pinned

concat_gap.assessment: The same function.zip and the same part ID (0xd40) ran on both sides, so neither a code change nor a part-ID mix explains the gap. Within Lambda the share is similar on both parts that were sampled (run 1: 5.27% on 0xd40, 5.93% on 0xd0c; run 2: 5.64% and 6.47%), so it is not specific to one part. Two method differences remain: offline gave 2.65% under the same sampler and 1.16% under perf, so the tool alone moves it by about 2x; and Lambda vs offline differ in unrecorded host conditions (kernel 5.10 in Lambda vs 6.1 offline, cgroup CPU quota, core count). Same sampler, same part: 5.64% vs 2.65%. Not attributable to code from this evidence; it stays open until hostinfo-instrumented Lambda rows exist to compare host conditions.

decision.meaning: Lambda assigns each new execution environment a CPU part the function cannot choose. Every run drew more than one part, the share of each part changes from run to run and between start classes, and the same request's engine time differs by part. A part is fixed for the life of one environment (no environment reported two). Comparisons are therefore valid only within one part and only between arms measured in the same rounds; pooled medians and cross-run comparisons carry the part mix.
rules_for_experiments: compare arms within each CPU part (summarize.by_cpu / engine_by_cpu_part) and report the part mix
interleave or alternate arms within the same rounds; never compare against another run's numbers without stratifying by part
report rows with no recorded part as unassessed, never as a shared stratum
a CPU-bound phase (engine, model_load_mmap, restore first request) moves with the part; an I/O phase (weight_download) need not, but must be checked per part before pooling
limits: a single part per environment proves nothing about the physical host or AZ; neither is observable
feature flags, HWCAPs, cgroup limits and kernel are unrecorded for every source run; the new hostinfo instrument records them for future runs
0xd4f appeared in cold rows of every run and in E6's warm rows, never in a restore wave or a snapshot-building init
invocations are clustered by environment and round, so per-invocation counts overstate the independent sample size; environment counts are given beside them

host_variability.assessment: Placement not controlled: 3 CPU part IDs (0xd0c, 0xd40, 0xd4f) across 10 runs, 10 of them drew every part; no environment changed part. 17 of 188 within-run arm comparisons have a pooled delta that a part-mix difference moved beyond the noise floor (sign_flip or mix_shift).
